toc.title: Why safety can be hard to reach
Point one: mindless coping with moderate to severe dysregulation
Point two: safety cues with mild dysregulation
Point three: safety anchoring while allowing defensive activation
Point four: deep immersion in safety
Wherever you are on the spectrum

blocks.p: The ventral vagal safety state of the Polyvagal Theory may not be easily accessible, especially if you exist in a traumatized state. And it's maybe even more difficult to deeply settle into it and experience it for extended periods of time. Let's look at what the safety state is, [the spectrum](piece:safety-vs-coping) of how it can be used, and when to use each part. This will give you a framework for where you're at, what you can handle, and your next steps.

According to the Polyvagal Theory, the ventral vagal safety state is the state of your body when it's prepared to connect: with others, with yourself, with the present moment. It's all about connection. The safety state uses the ventral vagal pathways of the parasympathetic autonomic nervous system.

The safety state is active when you're safe in a safe environment, when you're with safe others, or even when you're in solitude, alone but safe. It evolved within us in order to connect with each other. Mammals require connection. We rely on each other, and the safety state is the thing that facilitates that.

The safety state is also responsible for "health and growth and restoration," which is something the Polyvagal Theory's creator, Dr. Stephen Porges, says so often. That means it's responsible for self-regulation, homeostasis. The safety state optimizes our body's resources. It uses them for health and growth and restoration rather than for defense.

blocks.h: Why safety can be hard to reach

blocks.p: For some people, the safety state is not easily accessible. Day in, day out, they might have very little contact with their safety pathways, if any. That depends on the context of your current life, but also on your past.

If you're currently living with someone who is actually dangerous, or emotionally manipulative, or toxic, that's going to really challenge your ability to access your safety state. It probably won't happen in that context.

It also depends on how your past impacts your current state. You might be stuck in a state of defense: flight, fight, shutdown, freeze. You might have been stuck there for years at this point, maybe even decades. It could potentially last a very long time.

If you're stuck in a defensive state, accessing your safety state is a lot more challenging. You do access it at times. But when you do, it's extremely uncomfortable, and it's lost really easily. Or other emotions come along with it that need to be felt, like sadness, or abandonment, or shame. All kinds of stuff from your past is going to come up that needs to be felt. So when you access safety, you easily lose it.
Irene Lyon described this when she was on the podcast:

q: The moment the safety comes up, what does it allow the system to do? It allows it to express all the stored stuff that has been in there forever.

blocks.p: I've been playing around with this idea of a safety state spectrum. What does it look like when we have zero safety, and how do we deal with that, all the way over to tons of safety, and how do we get that? In my mind it makes sense as a spectrum, with four points:

ol: Mindless coping with moderate to severe dysregulation.
Safety anchoring to deeply immerse in your safety state.

blocks.h: Point one: mindless coping with moderate to severe dysregulation

blocks.p: At this point there's no significant safety state activation, and the dysregulation is moderate to severe. It might feel like a panic attack, a high level of anger, high anxiety, or overwhelm. Not just a little bit of stress, but a lot of stress, to the point of overwhelm. Things could get worse, of course, but we'll call that moderate to severe dysregulation.

That means you're too far into your defensive state activation. If you're feeling panic, you probably have a really good amount of freeze going on in your system. If you're feeling angry, there's too much fight. If you're feeling high anxiety, there's probably too much flight. Overwhelm and stress are probably also freeze, I would argue.

Turning on the safety state from here is very challenging for anybody. So what you'll probably do, and have done, are mindless coping strategies. They probably involve distracting yourself, numbing the dysregulation, checking out, or focusing on something else: doom scrolling through social media, watching those one-minute reels, binge watching a series, overeating. Even reading can be a mindless way of dealing with dysregulation. Immersing yourself in reading endlessly can be a way to distract yourself from what's happening inside.

None of these are bad. I'm not saying they're bad. But they're not exactly activating the safety state. They might help reduce the dysregulation, but they don't really ground you in safety. If you're panicking and you turn to doom scrolling, that might help you cope with the panic. But that doesn't mean you're ready to have a real connection with somebody in that moment. The safety state is still probably not online enough.

They're also not really experiencing the present moment, because the safety state isn't on. That's why I call them mindless coping strategies. If there was safety state activation, the defensive activation wouldn't be as dysregulated or as out of control. It wouldn't be a mindless experience, and you probably wouldn't be trying to escape the defensive activation or numb it.

A lot of the people who come into my courses and my community are at this end of the spectrum. That's real. It's valid. We're not going to judge it or try to shut it down. Let's just recognize it for what it is. Maybe you can put a little point on your spectrum and say, "Yeah, this is where I'm at more often than not."

It may help to realize, then, that your capacity for immersing yourself in safety and connecting with yourself in the present moment is very limited right now. There's no need to judge it. Just recognize it, and maybe work on the next step on the spectrum.

blocks.h: Point two: safety cues with mild dysregulation

blocks.p: Cues are different from anchors, which I'll get to. Safety cues are mostly passive, and they can trigger your safety state. They help to turn it on. So safety cues might help reduce defensive state activation.

But safety cues are not like doom scrolling. A safety cue is something your senses pick up, like dimmed lighting, or a candle that provides a passive cue of safety through scent. Safety cues are great to have at all times, because they provide a nice platform of passive safety. You can also use them when it comes to mild dysregulation. If you're in moderate to severe dysregulation, they might still be kind of helpful, but I don't think they'll do a whole lot.

You can identify mild dysregulation because you'll have emotions that are uncomfortable, but for the most part tolerable. They're noticeable, but they're not too much: irritation, anxiety, frustration. They won't send you into a spiral of panic or overwhelm. Safety cues might help reduce the intensity of these defensive emotions.

The safety cues you use are preplanned. For the most part, they can just exist around you: the right type of lighting in your home, the right scents, the right music. They're just there, and they can help reduce defensive activation.

You can also use them in a more planned way. You can have a regulation station filled with things you know will help trigger your safety state. It might have that texture that just feels right, or that certain thing that reminds you of a happier time when you felt safe and connected, or the right smell. Things you can go to that help reduce the irritation or the anger or the mild stress.

So safety cues can be passive or active. You can have them in the environment, providing passive cues of safety, which I recommend pretty much all the time. And you can use them more actively by mindfully experiencing them, really focusing on what it's like to touch that blanket that feels right, or to smell that candle or that spray you like so much. It's passive because it's there, but you can focus on it and make it more active.

At this point on the spectrum, the goal is probably to reduce, or even eliminate, the defensive activation. You're not really welcoming it or trying to feel it. You're not making space to have safety and defense active at the same time. You're getting through the moment, but not with mindless coping. It's more mindful coping.

blocks.h: Point three: safety anchoring while allowing defensive activation

blocks.p: The point here is not to dismiss, reduce, eliminate, or ignore the defensive activation, but to actually allow it, and maybe even mindfully feel it if you can handle it, while you're anchored in safety. We're not trying to get rid of it. We're letting it be there.

So at this point, we're doing more than setting up passive safety cues. We're trying to settle more deeply into safety. We want to feel connection: with ourselves, with the external environment, maybe with somebody else through co-regulation, and even with the defensive activation itself.

This unlocks the ability to use pendulation: going from safety to defense, if you want to. You can feel your safety state, then choose to feel your defensive activation, then choose to go back to your safety state, like a bookend. At this point on the spectrum, you'd be able to recognize where your defensive activation lives within you, and where your safety lives within you as well.

Pendulation is really helpful, and actually pretty darn necessary, for titrating stuck trauma. Titration means releasing it a little bit at a time. Through pendulation, you can start to release stuck defensive activation a little at a time. Pendulation is really more for stuck freeze trauma, I would say. But allowing both safety and defense is also helpful for welcoming returning sympathetic activation, like coming out of shutdown into fight.

This point on the spectrum is also helpful, maybe even necessary, for building the strength of your vagal brake. The vagal brake is the influence of your safety state on your heart. It helps keep your heartbeat at a calmer pace, even in the face of what would otherwise be dysregulating. So it's the ability to tolerate more defensive activation without losing access to your safety state. Allowing defense and safety, and going back and forth between them, helps build your capacity, the strength of your vagal brake.

But at this point, you really already have to have a good amount of safety. You need a strong enough vagal brake to allow the defensive activation without getting sucked into it. At the beginning of the spectrum, there was almost no safety state activation. Now, at point three, it takes a pretty good amount.

So if you're just starting out on your trauma recovery journey, and you notice you're constantly in a defensive state and you can't allow it while being safe, that's probably because your vagal brake just isn't strong enough yet. It may have nothing to do with you, your value as a human being, or how weak or strong you are. It's more about your safety state and its ability to tolerate defense.

It is possible to get here by practicing point two: having safety cues and experiencing them. As you practice that and build the strength of your safety state, eventually you'll be able to be in defense and safety at the same time.

And when you can do that, the defensive activation won't be dysregulating, and it won't really be a hindrance to you. It'll be there, but you'll still be able to function. You'll be able to have compassion for your defensive activation while you live a normal life and do whatever you need to do. It won't be as disruptive to your daily functioning, maybe not at all.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: Point four: deep immersion in safety

blocks.p: At the other end of the spectrum is using safety anchoring to deeply immerse yourself in your safety state: a much fuller, more robust experience of safety and connection.

When you're deep enough in it, you can have connection with yourself, with your inner world, all of it. Not just the good stuff, but also the stuff that doesn't feel so good. You'll have connection with the present moment and your senses. And you'll potentially have connection with other people, or other mammals, like your pets.

When you're deep enough in your safety state, you can comfortably access the mixed states of play and stillness. You can be silly and be okay with it. Someone in my community said she allows herself to feel silliness when she's deeply enough immersed in her safety state. You can also access stillness, which is the ability to be immobile and be okay with it.

From here, you can meditate and be curious about your inner world without judgment. You can allow whatever is inside of you to be there, without judgment and without fear, and feel it with compassion. That even includes defensive activation, and even stuck trauma that might still reside within you.
You'll have an appreciation for life and for other people. For me, what comes up a lot is appreciation, and this experience of awe, of really existing.

Connection isn't scary here. Before this point, the idea of connection can be terrifying. Someone else in my community said even the word connection is terrifying for her. But when you're deep in your safety state, you're not scared of it. You actually have an impulse to connect with others, with yourself, with the environment. You seek it out without choosing to. Your body is just ready for it.

It's very difficult to get this deep into safety. It requires that you purposefully practice and mindfully experience your safety state, then allow and feel defensive activation, build the strength of your vagal brake, and then go even deeper into safety. It's a long process, and it requires a really strong safety state.

blocks.h: Wherever you are on the spectrum

blocks.p: When you hear people say "don't let your joy go," or "find things that make you happy," "have healthy boundaries," "empower yourself," all of those things come from a really strong safety state. If you're not there yet, that's okay. It just means you're not there yet.

You're still progressing on the spectrum toward points three and four. Your body does want to allow safety and defense to exist at the same time. Your body does want to have deep moments of connection with yourself, with other people, and with the present moment. It wants to naturally self-regulate in that direction. It has to. As an organism, that's what it evolved to do.
So you might not be that far along on your spectrum, and that's okay. The word "yet" is really important here.

No matter where you're at, practicing being in safety is very important. Setting yourself up with passive safety cues in your environment is very important. Mindfully having little micro moments of connection can be helpful. That might just be using your senses to detect what feels more good versus more bad, to put it very simply. And eventually, the stuckness in your system will get less.
